prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose, with a poetic foundation, that turns memory, the body and dream into a sustained inner cosmos

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Cărtărescu, a single writer in Romanian. What round 1 changed is the wording and the weighting. The case rests on the common criteria. His voice is unmistakable. The prose is densely patterned and long-breathed. The Orbitor sequence (Blinding is its first volume) and Solenoid, as publicly described, treat memory, the body and dream as a single imaginative system and not as a series of topics. I read that as formal ambition joined to real intellectual depth. The major structures are finished and can be assessed as an oeuvre now. The citation should be prose-centred and name the poetry as foundation and part of the oeuvre. That reflects what the committee can actually weigh, since the colleagues who raised the point, Carlberg and Olsson among them, cannot establish the poetry's separate weight and neither can I. I do not use the identical opening rankings as an argument. The case holds because the architecture looks cumulative and the voice is sustained across decades, and I mean that as a provisional judgment from public knowledge. I have not verified the corpus independently and I cannot assess Romanian sentence texture directly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and not resolved by discussion. The linguistic achievement lies in Romanian rhythm, syntax and density, so any statement about style is provisional for me and for the committee. Scale may hide unevenness in the later volumes. Nobody has shown from the texts that the late work advances the project and does not merely enlarge it. The claim for the poetry and early work is thin, so the 'poetic foundation' wording must not imply a verdict the evidence cannot support. If Romanian-reading expert reports showed that the sentence-level effect is thin or that the late volumes repeat the earlier ones, the case would weaken. Adonis, on formal renewal of a whole poetic language, or Can Xue, on radical narrative singularity, would then deserve a harder look. I keep both as live alternatives for that reason and not out of courtesy.

responses.point: Olsson reads Solenoid and the later works as extending rather than repeating the earlier project. He asks the committee to test whether the later volumes advance the project or only enlarge it, and he would rest the citation on the prose alone if the poetry cannot be shown to carry weight.
responses.response: I accept his test as the right one and treat his reading as plausible but unverified. I cannot name specific volumes whose quality I have confirmed, and I will not invent evidence for it. What I can say is that the structure of the multi-part work, with its returns and enlargements, gives the committee something concrete to examine. I side with his fallback on the citation. The wording I propose names the poetry as a foundation and puts the weight on the prose. If expert readers found the poetry weaker or stronger than assumed, the wording should be adjusted. The laureate should not change on that account.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Adonis second and calls him a strong alternative but not a firm first choice, because judging Arabic prosody and diction through selective translation is a limit for everyone. She asks me for a concrete account of which works carry an oeuvre-level case for Tawada.
responses.response: I agree that Adonis's case lies in the poems and the poetics, and that essays and public positions have no weight in it. On Tawada I concede the point. I cannot name a decisive work-level argument that survives the evidentiary limits we have named, because her method needs a reader in both Japanese and German and the translated corpus is partial and weighted toward fiction. That is why I keep her out of my alternatives. The estrangement between her two languages is a formal principle and not a biographical detail. But I cannot demonstrate sustained quality across her genres, and I will not ask the committee to prefer her on that basis. Adonis remains my first alternative, conditional on stronger Arabic-reading evidence than we now have.

responses.point: Palm ranks Can Xue second for radical originality and says it is unresolved whether decades in one dream-logic mode deepen it or repeat it. She also doubts that Adonis's influence as critic and anthologist should be mistaken for the intrinsic quality of his poems.
responses.response: On Adonis she is right that influence is not intrinsic quality, and I agree the argument must be made from the poems themselves. I cannot supply that argument from translation, which is why he is an alternative and not my first choice. On Can Xue I still hold what I said in round 1. The formal radicalism is integral to her vision, and nobody has yet shown development within the mode. If Palm or Sward can point to particular works where the method deepens or changes, I would take that seriously. Without it, the multi-volume pattern of accumulation and return gives Cărtărescu a visible advantage on sustained quality, and I would say that this is an asymmetry of evidence and not a verdict that his work is better.

responses.point: Sward says the asymmetry of evidence between Cărtărescu's multi-volume structure and Can Xue's partial translated corpus, and not a different estimate of quality, is why she places Can Xue behind him for now. She also notes that Carson's English-language voice can be judged directly.
responses.response: I share that framing. Our ordering reflects what we can examine and not a settled comparison of merit, and we should say so openly. Her point about Carson is fair, and I respect that direct access to the language is a real advantage in judging voice. My reservation is the one I gave Mattson in round 1. A significant share of her work is translation, adaptation and intertextual response, and the committee has not yet defined what counts as the original oeuvre. Until the scope of a Carson citation is defined, I cannot support her over a writer with a clean oeuvre. That is not a judgment on her formal invention, which I find real.

uncertainties: No member, including me, has independently verified the texts. Every judgment rests on public knowledge, and the sentence-level achievement in Romanian, Arabic and Chinese is judged only indirectly.
Whether the later volumes of Orbitor and Solenoid, and the later novels, advance the project or only enlarge it remains unverified. I cannot name volumes that settle it.
The separate weight of Cărtărescu's poetry and early work is unestablished, and the 'poetic foundation' wording in the citation is a drafting choice and not a literary finding.

Whether Can Xue's sustained mode develops, whether Adonis's poems carry the case without his critical influence, and what counts as Carson's original oeuvre are all unresolved with the evidence before us.
Translation coverage is partial and uneven across all non-English candidates, and expert Romanian, Arabic or Chinese readings could change the comparisons.
Carlberg's simulated vote rests on a modelling assumption about her committee status, and this round models a recommendation and not the full Academy's decision.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile: no personal, institutional or editorial tie to any shortlisted writer is documented. My own interests in Central Europe and documentary historical fiction are literary context, not evidence of a preference. Collegial ties (elected alongside Ingrid Carlberg in 2020; service with Olsson, Mattson, Swärd and Palm) involve no candidate. This is a reading of the supplied profile and not an independently verified statement.
